title: Roles of Primary Health Care Workers
path: Roles of Primary Health Care Workers

headings.title: Introduction to Primary Health Care Workforce in Nigeria
headings.content: The Primary Health Care (PHC) workforce in Nigeria forms the bedrock of the national healthcare delivery system, designed to bring comprehensive, equitable, and cost-effective health services as close as possible to where people live and work. Operating primarily at the grassroots level through a network of comprehensive and basic health centers, this diverse cadre of health professionals addresses the most prevalent health problems in the community by providing promotive, preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services. The structural framework of the Nigerian PHC system relies heavily on a team-based approach, where different cadres of workers integrate their distinct skills to manage endemic diseases, maternal and child health issues, and basic sanitation challenges. Understanding the specific roles, training backgrounds, and scopes of practice of these healthcare workers is essential for student nurses. It ensures effective delegation, seamless coordination, and optimization of health outcomes within resource-constrained environments. As frontline providers, PHC workers also serve as the vital first point of contact between the populace and the formal health sector, bridging cultural and geographical gaps to foster community ownership and sustainable health development across both rural and urban settlements in Nigeria.

headings.title: Community Physicians
headings.content: Community Physicians, often medical officers assigned to local government areas or comprehensive health centers, play a critical leadership and clinical role within the Primary Health Care system in Nigeria. As medically qualified practitioners, they are responsible for diagnosing and managing complex medical cases that exceed the scope of nurses and community health extension workers. Beyond direct patient care, community physicians provide technical supervision, clinical mentorship, and continuous professional guidance to the multidisciplinary PHC team. They oversee disease surveillance programs, coordinate responses to local epidemic outbreaks, and design community-specific health promotion strategies based on epidemiological data. Their presence ensures that evidence-based medical standards are maintained at the grassroot level. Furthermore, community physicians act as a vital administrative and clinical link, facilitating the referral of complicated cases from primary health facilities to secondary and tertiary hospitals. By collaborating closely with nurses, CHOs, and local leaders, community physicians help bridge clinical medicine and public health practice, ensuring that healthcare delivery remains comprehensive, safe, and responsive to the unique health vulnerabilities of the rural and semi-urban populations they serve.

headings.title: Community Health Officers (CHOs)
headings.content: Community Health Officers (CHOs) are middle-level health management personnel who occupy a pivotal supervisory and administrative position within Nigeria's Primary Health Care system. Typically trained as advanced community health practitioners, CHOs act as the bridge between lower-level health workers, such as Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs), and higher medical authorities. Their core responsibilities include managing Primary Health Care facilities, supervising clinic operations, and ensuring the smooth implementation of primary health care programs like immunization, maternal care, and health education. CHOs possess advanced training in clinical diagnosis, minor ailment treatment, and community diagnosis, enabling them to evaluate community health needs and plan localized interventions. They also play a crucial role in data collection, health management information systems (HMIS) reporting, and resource management at the facility level. By providing routine supportive supervision to junior staff, CHOs maintain high standards of clinical practice and service delivery. Their leadership within Basic Health Centers ensures that services remain accessible, effective, and compliant with national health policies, making them indispensable pillars in the architectural design of Nigeria's grassroots healthcare framework.

headings.title: Public Health Nurses
headings.content: Public Health Nurses (PHNs) are specialized nursing professionals who focus on the health of entire communities and populations rather than just treating individual patients. Within the Nigerian Primary Health Care structure, PHNs are instrumental in planning, implementing, and evaluating community-based disease prevention and health promotion programs. Their core duties encompass organizing mass immunization campaigns, conducting school health programs, monitoring environmental sanitation, and providing comprehensive maternal and child health (MCH) services, including family planning and antenatal care. PHNs also play a leading role in epidemiological surveillance by tracking disease outbreaks, managing contact tracing, and educating the populace on communicable and non-communicable disease prevention. Because they possess advanced training in public health principles, they collaborate with community leaders to identify health deficits, mobilize local resources, and design culturally appropriate health education interventions. Furthermore, Public Health Nurses serve as educators and advocates, empowering individuals and families with self-care knowledge to improve overall community resilience. Their expertise ensures that preventive and promotive healthcare strategies are executed efficiently across diverse Nigerian communities.

headings.title: Midwives
headings.content: Midwives are frontline maternal and child health specialists whose primary mandate is to ensure safe pregnancy, childbirth, and postnatal recovery for mothers and newborns in the Primary Health Care setting. In Nigeria, where maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality rates remain significant public health concerns, midwives play an irreplaceable role in delivering life-saving interventions at the grassroots level. Their responsibilities include conducting thorough antenatal assessments, identifying high-risk pregnancies, managing normal spontaneous vaginal deliveries, and providing immediate essential newborn care, including resuscitation when necessary. Midwives also provide comprehensive postnatal care to monitor involution, promote exclusive breastfeeding, and deliver vital family planning counseling. Operating often within Midwives Service Scheme (MSS) or primary health clinics in rural areas, they educate expectant mothers on nutrition, danger signs during pregnancy, and birth preparedness. When complications such as prolonged labor, postpartum hemorrhage, or severe pre-eclampsia arise, midwives are trained to initiate emergency stabilization and execute timely referrals to higher levels of care. Through compassionate and skilled clinical practice, midwives safeguard the foundational health of families and communities.

headings.title: Community Health Extension Workers (Senior and Junior)
headings.content: Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs), categorized into Senior CHEWs and Junior CHEWs (JCHEWs), form the largest numerical workforce in Nigeria's Primary Health Care delivery system, especially at the grassroots and village levels. Trained specifically for community-based healthcare delivery, Senior CHEWs undergo extensive professional preparation that enables them to diagnose and treat common ailments, provide antenatal care, conduct normal deliveries under supervision, and manage basic environmental health programs. They supervise Junior CHEWs and direct community mobilization efforts. Junior CHEWs, on the other hand, focus on foundational, preventive, and basic curative services, such as routine immunization, growth monitoring of children, basic health education, and treating minor ailments like uncomplicated malaria and diarrhea at the health post level. Both cadres act as agents of behavioral change, living and working within the communities they serve to bridge cultural divides and promote healthy lifestyles. They are crucial for implementing the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) strategies. By executing home visits, managing local health posts, and reporting disease outbreaks to higher authorities, CHEWs ensure that basic healthcare reaches the most remote and underserved populations.

headings.title: Village Health Workers
headings.content: Village Health Workers (VHWs) are voluntary, community-selected health agents who serve as the closest and most accessible link between the formal health system and remote rural households in Nigeria. Chosen directly by their community members, VHWs possess a deep understanding of local customs, languages, and health beliefs, making them uniquely positioned to foster trust and encourage health-seeking behaviors. Although they do not receive formal professional medical training, VHWs undergo short, practical orientations facilitated by public health nurses and CHEWs. Their primary responsibilities include promoting basic hygiene, distributing simple preventive commodities such as insecticide-treated nets, identifying common symptoms of prevalent illnesses like malaria and diarrhea, and providing basic first aid. They also mobilize community members for public health campaigns, such as polio immunizations and sanitation drives, and act as informal reporters of unusual disease occurrences to nearby primary health clinics. By empowering local populations with basic health literacy and encouraging prompt utilization of formal health facilities, Village Health Workers play a foundational role in achieving primary health care goals and ensuring grassroots community participation.

headings.title: Traditional Birth Attendants
headings.content: Traditional Birth Attendants (TBAs) are community-based practitioners who assist pregnant women during childbirth, drawing their knowledge from indigenous traditions, cultural beliefs, and apprenticeship-rather than formal Western medical education. In many rural Nigerian communities, TBAs remain highly influential and widely utilized due to their physical accessibility, cultural alignment, and affordability. Recognizing their pervasive role, modern public health strategies emphasize integrating and training TBAs rather than ignoring them. Trained TBAs are taught to recognize danger signs during pregnancy and labor-such as severe bleeding, prolonged labor, or malpresentations-and are strictly instructed to avoid harmful cultural practices like abdominal pressure. Their primary contribution to the Primary Health Care system lies in early identification of obstetric complications, promoting birth preparedness, and facilitating prompt referrals of high-risk women to formal health facilities staffed by midwives and doctors. By building collaborative relationships between TBAs and professional PHC workers, the health system can successfully reduce home-delivery complications, improve maternal tracking, and bridge the gap between traditional practices and safe modern obstetric care.

headings.title: Interprofessional Collaboration and Referral Systems in PHC
headings.content: Interprofessional collaboration and an effective referral system are the lifeblood of a functional Primary Health Care system in Nigeria, ensuring that patients receive continuous, safe, and appropriate care across different levels of the healthcare continuum. Because PHC relies on a diverse team of medical officers, nurses, midwives, CHOs, CHEWs, and community volunteers, clear communication, mutual respect, and defined scopes of practice are essential to prevent role confusion and minimize medical errors. Collaborative practice allows each cadre to contribute their unique expertise, creating a holistic care plan for patients. Hand-in-hand with teamwork is the referral system-a structured mechanism that ensures smooth patient transfer from lower-level health posts or basic health centers to comprehensive health centers, and ultimately to secondary or tertiary hospitals when specialized intervention is required. An effective referral chain depends on accurate documentation, timely communication, clear clinical handover, and accessible transportation networks. For student nurses, mastering this collaborative and referral dynamic is vital, as nurses often act as coordinators who assess patient needs, stabilize clients, and initiate timely transfers, thereby reducing morbidity and mortality through a united healthcare front.
